In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surah ʿAbasa (He Frowned)

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He frowned and turned away﴾ ﴿because the blind man came to him.﴾

The occasion of revelation of this surah is agreed upon by the exegetes: that he (ﷺ) was occupied with calling the chieftains of Quraysh, when Ibn Umm Maktum, who was a blind man, came to him and said: "Teach me, O Messenger of Allah, and instruct me in what Allah has taught you," and he repeated that. But that did not fit with what he (ﷺ) was occupied with, and with what he hoped for, which was greater, so he frowned and turned away from him, being busy with what he was engaged in.

The Shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him, said, in removing the appearance of inconsistency regarding His saying, ﴿because the blind man came to him﴾, the following: Exalted is He, He referred to this noble Companion, who is ʿAbd Allah ibn Umm Maktum, by a title that people dislike, even though He said: ﴿And do not insult one another by nicknames﴾ [al-Hujurat: 11].

The answer is what some scholars have pointed out: that the secret in describing him with the word "the blind" is to indicate his excuse for interrupting the speech of the Messenger (ﷺ), because if he had been able to see what he was occupied with among the chieftains of the disbelievers, he would not have interrupted his speech. End of his words verbatim.

Al-Fakhr al-Razi said: Although he was blind and could not see, he could hear, and by hearing the speech of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and by his intrusion upon his interruption of it, he would be committing a sin, so how could the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) be rebuked for it?

His statement here indicates that if he was excused for not seeing, he was not excused for being able to hear; but He mentioned him by his description so as to call for compassion toward him and gentleness with him.

And the apparent meaning, and Allah knows best, is that al-Razi's words are not far from what the Shaykh mentioned, because their meaning is that He rebuked him for his lack of gentleness toward him and his failure to consider his state of blindness.

Accordingly, mentioning him with this description is by way of allusion to others, the chieftains and nobles of the people, and it is as if He is saying to them: ﴿For indeed it is not the eyes that are blinded, but the hearts within the breasts are blinded﴾ (p-٤٣١) [al-Hajj: 46]. This man is blind in sight, but keen of insight: he saw the truth and believed, and came with his blindness striving for more, while you, your hearts are closed and your insights are blinded, so you did not perceive the reality and did not see the light of faith, as in the noble verse: ﴿For indeed it is not the eyes that are blinded, but the hearts within the breasts are blinded.﴾

And knowledge is with Allah, exalted is He.

Note.

What the scholars of hadith agreed upon is the permissibility of mentioning such descriptions when they are for identification and not for belittling. So they said: al-Aʿma (the blind), al-Aʿwar (the one-eyed), al-Aʿraj (the lame). And regarding crafts they said: al-Kharraz (the leatherworker), al-Kharaqi, and the like. This is because there is benefit in identifying the men in the chain of narration (isnad).

Such a thing is not mutual insult by nicknames in this discipline. And Allah knows best.

And likewise, when it is for identification with a sound purpose and without disparagement, as we have stated.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He frowned and turned away﴾, there is in it a similar matter to His saying: ﴿because the blind man came to him﴾, because frowning is something that does not apparently fit with His saying concerning him (ﷺ): ﴿And indeed you are of a great moral character﴾ [al-Qalam: 4], and His saying: ﴿And lower your wing to the believers﴾ [al-Hijr: 88]. I have not found an answer to this, and the Shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him, did not address it in removing the appearance of inconsistency.

What appears, and Allah knows best, is that this does not arise with it, because he (ﷺ) did not speak anything that would harm this Companion within himself, with something he would hear and be disturbed by. All that came from him (ﷺ) was a furrowing of the brow, and this is a visible movement, not an audible one.

And the situation is that this man, being blind, did not see that movement, so it is as if he did not encounter any harm from him (ﷺ).

Furthermore, he (ﷺ) was content with him because of the good that he had in his religion. As he said concerning Hunayn: "And I entrust some people to what is in their hearts," meaning, when he gave to those whose hearts were to be reconciled (al-Muallafa Qulubuhum), and did not give the Ansar what is well known in the story, so Allah did not rebuke him for that. And the Ansar were pleased and wept from joy and contentment.

Moreover, the furrowing of the brow and the relaxing of the lines of the face, for grief or for joy, is almost innate in what came from him (ﷺ), so it is by way of innateness approximately, as if what provoked it was a general matter arising from the specific nature of the Message and its mission.

Nevertheless, it has come from him (ﷺ) that after its revelation he would say to him: "Welcome to the one about whom my Lord rebuked me," and would honor him, and he appointed him as deputy over Madinah twice.

On this basis, the intended meaning here is two matters:

The first: the elevation of his (ﷺ) character to a limitless degree, to the point of a glance with the eye and a furrowing of the brow, even toward one who does not see it, as he (ﷺ) said: "It is not befitting for a Prophet to have the treachery of the eyes" (Khaʾinat al-Aʿyun), and that was in the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah.

The second: a discipline for the Ummah and for callers to Islam in particular, through the person of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), just as He taught them through his person regarding kindness to parents, in His saying: ﴿If one of them or both of them reach old age with you, do not say to them "uff," nor scold them﴾ [al-Isra: 23].

This whole context from the beginning of the surah to His saying: ﴿No! Indeed it is a reminder﴾ ﴿so whoever wills may remember it﴾ [ʿAbasa: 11-12] is an explanation, because the Messenger (ﷺ) does not give preference in calling to Allah to the rich over the poor, and he should be patient with the weak among the believers; for the Message is conveyance, and there is no responsibility upon him beyond that, so he should not burden himself for them.

And Allah, exalted is He, urged him to patience with the believers because of their faith, in His saying: ﴿And keep yourself patient with those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His face, and do not let your eyes pass beyond them, desiring the adornment of the worldly life; and do not obey one whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance, who follows his desire and whose affair is ever excess﴾ ﴿And say: The truth is from your Lord, so whoever wills let him believe, and whoever wills let him disbelieve﴾ [al-Kahf: 28-29].

Similar to this is His saying: ﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His face. Nothing of their account is upon you, and nothing of your account is upon them, so that you would drive them away and thus be among the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Anʿam: 52].

The Shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him, had previously presented some of this explanation at this verse, and he showed that this admonition was given by the Prophet of Allah Nuh to his people, when they looked down upon the weak among the believers, in His saying: ﴿So the chiefs of those who disbelieved among his people said: "We do not see you but a human like ourselves, and we do not see those who follow you except the lowest of us in judgment at first glance"﴾ up to His saying ﴿"And I will not drive away those who believe. Indeed, they will meet their Lord, but I see you as a people who are ignorant"﴾ [Hud: 27-29].

This verse and its like indicate the truthfulness of the statement of Heraclius, when he asked Abu Sufyan about the followers of Muhammad (ﷺ): "Are they the nobles of the people or their weak?" He said: "Rather, their weak." He said: "Thus are the followers of the Messengers."

The scholars said regarding this: because they are closer to the natural disposition (fitrah), and further from authority and rank, so they have no greed for a position that would be lost, nor for a status that would be wasted, and they find in religion honor and elevation. Thus were Bilal, Suhayb, and ʿAmmar, and thus was Ibn Umm Maktum, may Allah be pleased with them all.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 80, verse 2:

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

(p-433) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surah 'Abasa (He Frowned)

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That the blind man came to him.﴾

Allah, may He be exalted, referred to this noble Companion, who is 'Abd Allah ibn Umm Maktum, by a nickname that people dislike, although He Himself said: ﴿And do not insult one another by nicknames﴾ [al-Hujurat: 11].

The answer is what some scholars have pointed out: that the secret in describing him with the word "the blind man" (al-a'ma) is to indicate his excuse for interrupting the speech of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), because if he had seen the people he was occupied with, namely the leading unbelievers, he would not have cut off his speech.

**The Word of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿As for he who thinks himself self-sufficient,﴾ ﴿to him you give attention.﴾ ﴿And it is not upon you that he does not purify himself.﴾**

This is a statement of the Prophet's (ﷺ) attitude toward the whole Ummah, and of his eagerness for the Islam of all of them, even of one who turns away and considers himself self-sufficient, out of compassion and mercy toward them. Allah, the Exalted, described his state (ﷺ) in His saying: ﴿It grieves him that you suffer; he is eager for you﴾ [At-Tawbah: 128], and in His saying: ﴿Perhaps you would consume yourself with grief over their traces if they do not believe in this discourse﴾ [Al-Kahf: 6].

• His saying: ﴿And it is not upon you that he does not purify himself﴾ is a statement that the Prophet (ﷺ) bears no responsibility for one who does not purify himself. Allah, the Exalted, made this explicit in His saying: ﴿You are only a warner﴾ [Ar-Ra'd: 7],

• and His saying: ﴿Your duty is only to convey﴾ [Ash-Shura: 48],

• and His saying: ﴿Their guidance is not upon you﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 272],

and the like of these.

Allah has combined both matters from both sides in His saying, concerning Nuh (peace be upon him): ﴿I am not one to drive away the believers; I am only a clear warner﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara': 114–115].

"Indeed, no! Verily it is a reminder. So whoever wills may remember it, in scriptures held in honour, exalted and purified, by the hands of scribes, noble and righteous." (Quran 80:11-16)

It is known that the word "Kalla" (no, indeed not): it is a rebuke for what preceded, and it is, in its entirety, directed at the one who showed concern for the wealthy man, who insisted upon them and was eager to hear from him. But Allah the Exalted says: the station of the Qur'an, the Revelation and the religion is loftier than being offered to a people in this condition. It is, in its state, of honour, elevation, purity and protection, and what is with it of guardians, scribes, noble and righteous, is more deserving that one should seek it, and the good is for the one who comes to it seeking it.

"So whoever wills may remember it." This is for threat, not for choice, as shown by what follows: "Woe to man, how ungrateful he is!" (Quran 80:17). "Woe to man" (qutila al-insan): a supplication against him; and "al-insan" refers to the disbelieving kind; and "ma akfarahu" (how ungrateful he is): that is, how intense is his disbelief in it, after all of this, given the exaltedness of its station.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 80, verse 17:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Destroyed be man, how ungrateful he is!﴾ It has been said: ﴿how ungrateful he is!﴾ here means "how much he disbelieves" (ma af'alahu), i.e., how intense his kufr (disbelief/ingratitude) is.

Al-Zamakhshari (the author of al-Kashshaf) said: it is an expression of wonder at his excess in being ungrateful for the blessings of Allah.

It has also been said: "What thing moved him to denial and disbelief?" All of these meanings are possible.

The first meaning is probably the most apparent, because of His saying before it: ﴿Destroyed be man﴾, and because this meaning occurs in other places: ﴿Indeed, man is greatly unjust and ungrateful﴾ [Ibrahim: 34]. Likewise, fa'ul (the pattern of intensity) occurs in His saying: ﴿And it is He who gave you life and then causes you to die and then gives you life again. Indeed, man is ungrateful﴾ [al-Hajj: 66]. This is also the description of those who deny the signs of Allah, as in His saying: ﴿And none rejects Our signs except every treacherous ingrate﴾ [Luqman: 32].

Then Allah, exalted is He, refutes him by returning him to the origin of his creation, so that he may take admonition from himself, in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿From what thing did He create him?﴾ ﴿From a sperm-drop He created him and determined him.﴾ ﴿Then He made the way easy for him.﴾ ﴿Then He causes him to die and puts him in a grave.﴾ [Abasa: 18-21]; because these three are agreed upon, and He arranged upon them the fourth: ﴿Then, when He wills, He will resurrect him.﴾ [Al-Ma'arij: 22].

As for His saying: ﴿From a sperm-drop He created him and determined him﴾, the explanation of the origin of human creation and its stages has preceded many times.

As for His saying: ﴿Then He made the way easy for him﴾, it has been said: "the way" refers to his exit from his mother's womb, when He turned his head toward the direction of exit, instead of what he was upon, facing upward. This is among the facilitation of his path of exit. This is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and others, and it is the preference of Ibn Jarir.

And it has been said: "the way" means the religion in its clarity and the ease of acting upon it, like His saying, exalted is He: (p-435) ﴿Indeed, We guided him to the way, either grateful or ungrateful﴾ [Al-Insan: 3]. This is narrated from al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd, and Ibn Kathir preferred it.

Perhaps what Ibn Kathir preferred is the more preponderant, because facilitating birth is a matter common to every animal, and it is observed and tangible, so there is no distinction for man in it over others. Just as what precedes it indicates it, or indicates its implication, which is power, in His saying: ﴿From a sperm-drop He created him and determined him﴾.

The facilitation of birth may also fall under His saying: "and determined him", i.e., He determined his forming, the time of his existence, the time of his exit, the measures of his body, the measure of his life, and the measure of his death, as is known.

As for facilitating the way of religion, it is what is specific to man, and it is what is required to turn toward, and it is what relates to other than him between his being formed from a sperm-drop and his determination, and between his causing to die and his burial. That is, the period of his life in this world; i.e., He created him from a sperm-drop and determined his coming into this world, and made the religion easy for him in its obligations. Then He caused him to die so that He might see what he did: ﴿Then, when He wills, He will resurrect him.﴾

And for this reason, at the conclusion, He said: ﴿Nay, he has not yet fulfilled what He commanded him.﴾ [Abasa: 23]. And there is nothing here that indicates the command except "the way He made easy." And Allah, exalted is He, knows best.

The commentary, having first explained for man what he was created from, now explains how He provides him with food, and in both there is a sign of power.

The two verses share three matching stages. The pouring of water from the sky onto the earth corresponds to the emission of water into the womb. The splitting of the earth for plants corresponds to the emergence of the child into the world. The growing of the various kinds of plants corresponds to the different measures of creation.

By specifying the kinds of plants: grain, fresh herbage (qadb), grapes, pomegranates, olives, palm trees, various fruits, and dense walled gardens, the meaning of diversity in them becomes evident, even though they come from two common sources: the water from the sky, and the soil in the earth, which is irrigated with one water.

Once more, it is said to the Communists and the Dahriyyin (materialists who deny a Creator): ﴿Destroyed is man, how ungrateful he is!﴾ ﴿From what thing did He create him?﴾ [Abasa: 17–18] (p-436) ﴿Have you considered what you emit? Is it you who create it, or are We the Creator? We have decreed death among you, and We are not to be outdone, in that We replace your likenesses and bring you into being in what you do not know. And you have certainly known the first creation, so will you not remember? Have you considered what you plant? Is it you who make it grow, or are We the grower? If We willed, We would make it into debris.﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 58–65].

Without doubt, they do not claim for themselves the doing of any of that. Indeed, they know that it has a Creator who manages it, but they are stubborn. ﴿And they denied them, though their souls were convinced of them, out of injustice and arrogance.﴾ [al-Naml: 14]. God the Mighty has spoken truly, and every sinful disbeliever has lied.

The Shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him, has already explained the creation of man in several earlier passages, the last of which is in Surat al-Rahman: ﴿He created man from clay like pottery.﴾ [al-Rahman: 14], and he has explained man's food in each of Surat al-Waqi'ah and Surat al-Jathiyah.

Allah's statement: ﴿Faces that Day will be radiant﴾ ﴿laughing, rejoicing.﴾

Al-Isfar (إسفار) is illumination, and it is the brightening of the face with joy, as Allah says: ﴿And He will give them radiance and joy﴾ [al-Insan: 11]. Al-Istibshar (استبشار) comes from the preceding glad tidings in His statement: ﴿The angels descend upon them, [saying], "Do not fear and do not grieve, but receive good tidings of Paradise, which you were promised."﴾ [Fussilat: 30].

And His statement: ﴿The Day you will see the believing men and believing women, their light running before them and on their right, [and it will be said], "Good tidings for you today: gardens beneath which rivers flow."﴾ [al-Hadid: 12].

The Shaykh (may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him) has already presented the explanation of this in the surah "al-Hadid."

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 80, verse 40:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And on that Day there will be faces, upon them dust,﴾ ﴿overcast by darkness.﴾ Allah, exalted is He, made clear that they are the disbelievers (al-kafarah) and the wicked (al-fajarah).

The explanation of this was already given by the Shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him, in surah "al-Rahman," in the discussion of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The criminals will be known by their marks﴾ [al-Rahman: 41].

Here He has combined for them disbelief and wickedness. These are disbelief in belief and wickedness in deeds, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they will not beget but a wicked disbelieving one﴾ [Nuh: 27]. And Allah, exalted is He, knows best.
